claim_review_spans.R1: Getting a 48 on your very first paper when you are used to doing well at home is a massive shock. It makes complete sense that you feel paralyzed right now and that dropping the class feels like the cleanest way to make the panic stop.
claim_review_spans.R2: Before you drop anything, let’s separate the immediate panic from what this mark actually means.
claim_review_spans.R3: You asked: *"I already changed the words from the readings. Isn't that my own writing then?"*
claim_review_spans.R4: The short answer is no, but **this is a classic cross-cultural academic misunderstanding, not proof that you can't handle university in English.**
claim_review_spans.R5: In many school systems, doing well means accurately summarizing and rewording the authorities or textbooks. In US universities, changing the words of the reading is considered mere *paraphrasing*. When a US professor asks for "your own argument," they do not mean just using your own vocabulary; they mean:
claim_review_spans.R6: *   What is your opinion or claim about the text?
claim_review_spans.R7: *   Do you agree, disagree, or interpret the evidence differently?
claim_review_spans.R9: You did not fail because your English is broken. You lost marks because you followed the rules of your previous school system instead of the unwritten rules of US academic writing. That is an entirely learnable skill, not an inherent flaw in your ability.
claim_review_spans.R10: Do not make a permanent decision about dropping the course tonight while your head is spinning. Instead, take these two concrete steps:
claim_review_spans.R11: Open your learning portal (Canvas, Blackboard, etc.) and look at the very top heading of that open assignment page.
claim_review_spans.R12: *   **If it belongs to the other class:** Close this tab for tonight. You don't have an emergency in *this* class tomorrow.
claim_review_spans.R13: *   **If it really is due tomorrow at 5:00 p.m. for this class:** Do not try to write a masterpiece tonight. Tomorrow morning, you can either request a short extension or visit the campus writing center.
claim_review_spans.R14: Dropping a class might seem like the easiest fix, but as an international student in your first semester in the US, **dropping below full-time enrollment (usually 12 credit hours for undergraduates) can severely threaten your legal student status.**
claim_review_spans.R15: Before you click "drop" on any portal:
claim_review_spans.R16: *   Check how many total credits you are enrolled in right now.
claim_review_spans.R17: *   Do not drop if it puts you under full-time status without speaking directly to your campus International Student Services office first.
claim_review_spans.R18: Professors in the US expect students to come to office hours when they receive a low grade, especially early in the semester. They respect students who want to understand the feedback.
claim_review_spans.R19: Here is a short, polite email you can copy, fill in, and send to request clarification:
claim_review_spans.R20: **Subject:** [Course Name/Number] - Question regarding Paper 1 feedback - [Your Full Name]
claim_review_spans.R21: Thank you for the feedback on my first paper. As an international student in my first semester here, I am still adapting to expectations around academic writing and developing an independent argument.
claim_review_spans.R22: I would really appreciate the opportunity to meet briefly during your office hours to make sure I understand how to approach the next assignment correctly. Could I stop by during your scheduled hours this week, or is there another time that works best for you?
claim_review_spans.R23: Thank you for your time and guidance.
claim_review_spans.R25: Take a slow breath. First assignments abroad are notoriously rough because no one explicitly teaches you the cultural difference in expectations until after you get a paper back. You are not stupid, and you are not in the wrong place. Check that deadline tab first, let the panic settle, and take it one step at a time.
